Usage Timeline (Timestamp Countdown).definition: The whole ad is paced by an on-screen clock or progress bar: it opens on the promise/first use, then each beat jumps forward in time (8:03pm > 8:14pm, or 5 sec > 15 min > 5 days > 2 weeks) with one caption saying what the product is doing at that moment, and closes on the end-state result + offer.
Usage Timeline (Timestamp Countdown).why: Turns a vague benefit into a concrete, believable sequence of milestones and makes viewers stay to see the final timestamp.
how: List 4-6 real milestones of using the product (first seconds, first session, day 5, week 2) with one benefit each.
Film or animate one shot per milestone with a big timestamp/progress bar overlay that advances every beat.
End on the final milestone result, then cut to product + offer card.
Usage Timeline (Timestamp Countdown).closest_existing: Challenge ('I tried X for 7 days') - this is not a creator challenge diary; the timer/progress bar itself is the structure and can run in minutes inside one session or as an animated graphic.

In-Store Find (Retail Aisle).definition: Shopper-POV video filmed inside a real, recognisable retailer: opens outside/at the shelf, the creator finds the product (or asks staff, who recommend it), shows the shelf, price tag and cart, then cuts home for close-ups and a 'grab it next time you're there / or online' close.
In-Store Find (Retail Aisle).why: Retail shelf presence borrows the store's credibility and signals 'this is a real mainstream brand', removing the 'random internet product' objection.
how: Only usable if the product is (or looks) stocked in a known store or a stockist boutique - film a POV walk to the shelf.
Show shelf, price tag, staff recommendation or the item going into the cart with captions on value.
Cut to home close-ups and end with 'in store or online, link below'.
In-Store Find (Retail Aisle).closest_existing: Product Demo / Day In The Life - here the setting (the retail aisle and the purchase moment) is the proof, not product use. Note: hard for pure dropshippers without retail placement.

Behind the Build (Factory / Process Tour.definition: A brand insider or a step-by-step sequence takes the viewer through where/how the product is made: opens on the finished product or the person on the factory/workshop floor, walks through materials, build and quality checks (often as numbered steps), and closes on the finished product in use or the reveal + brand card.
Behind the Build (Factory / Process Tour.why: Shows the craftsmanship and quality control behind the price, answering 'is it cheap junk / is it safe' objections with visible proof.
how: Get supplier/factory or workshop footage (ask your supplier for production-line clips) or film a rep in the warehouse.
Structure it as 3-4 steps: raw material > build > QC/packing, with one caption or line per step.
End on the finished product reveal or in use + offer.
Behind the Build (Factory / Process Tour.closest_existing: Pack An Order With Me (Fulfilment POV) - that shows packing a customer order; this shows manufacturing/quality of the product itself. Also unlike Founder Story, it is about the process, not the person's journey.

Product ASMR.definition: An 'ASMR' labelled ad with little or no voiceover: opens on the title + close-mic packaging sound, then a run of tactile sound moments (crinkle, pump, pour, lather, spray, crunch) using the product, closing on a calm end shot with the product.
Product ASMR.why: Sound-led sensory content is watched as entertainment, holds attention without a pitch and makes the product feel premium and satisfying.
how: Pick 5-8 sound-rich actions with the product (opening, pouring, applying, using).
Record close to a mic in a quiet room, no music or talking, and add a persistent 'ASMR' title overlay.
End on product hero shot + brand; keep it 10-35s.
Product ASMR.closest_existing: Satisfying B-roll (Front-Splice) - that is only a short visual hook spliced before a normal ad; here the whole ad is a sound-first ASMR routine with no pitch.

Panic Restock Reaction.definition: A ~10s single-shot meme: a creator holds the nearly empty product box with a shocked hand-over-mouth face under one caption ('why did I wait... it's almost gone AND almost sold out'), shows what's left, and that is the whole ad.
Panic Restock Reaction.why: Combines habit proof (she's used it up) with scarcity in one glance; cheap to make and reads as native content, best for warm/retargeting audiences.
how: Film a creator with an almost-used-up product (empty slots, last bottle) making a shocked/panic face.
Add one caption: 'I messed up... thought I had time, now I'm almost out and it's low stock'.
Keep it 8-12s, no VO; put the restock/low-stock offer in the copy.
Panic Restock Reaction.closest_existing: UGC Testimonial - no claims or story spoken; it is a silent reaction meme where the empty packaging + low-stock caption do the selling.

Phone-Screen Investigation.definition: A first-person 'I looked into it' story told almost entirely through phone screens: opens on a call screen or Google search ('I called my water company' / 'does legal water mean safe'), moves through real-looking web pages, databases, stats and a review card as evidence, then reveals the product as the fix with a before/after number and closes on the offer.
Phone-Screen Investigation.why: Screen evidence feels like the viewer's own research, so the problem reads as discovered fact rather than an ad claim; great for invisible-problem products.
how: Write the investigation as 5-7 'then I found...' beats tied to a hidden problem your product fixes.
Screen-record each step (call screen, Google search typing, a stat page, a lookup tool, a review) with one caption per beat.
Finish with the product shown solving it (number before > after) and an offer card.
Phone-Screen Investigation.closest_existing: Breakdown / Explainer - this is not a talking-head explanation; the whole ad is phone screen recordings acting as personal investigation evidence.

Brand Blunder Confession.definition: The brand opens by admitting a public mistake ('We f*cked up our spring sale'), proves it with a screen recording of the error and screenshots of angry/mocking customer comments, then 'makes it right' with an even bigger discount + free gifts and closes on urgency ('before we sell out').
Brand Blunder Confession.why: Self-deprecating honesty stops the scroll and the apology gives a believable reason for an unusually big discount.
how: Pick a real or plausible slip (wrong % live, typo, shipping delay) and open with a blunt confession caption.
Show proof: screen recording of the mistake + 3-5 customer comment screenshots roasting you.
Pivot to the make-good offer (bigger discount, gifts) with product b-roll and a sell-out urgency close.
Brand Blunder Confession.closest_existing: Reply To Question / Personal Update - here the hook is the brand's own public mistake and comment backlash, used as the reason-why for a sale.

Quiz Walkthrough.definition: A relatable person states a problem and the confusion ('hundreds of products... which one do I even need?'), says an expert built a short quiz, then a screen recording walks through the quiz questions and the 'calculating your results' screen, closing on 'take the free 2-minute quiz, link below'.
Quiz Walkthrough.why: Sells a free personalised answer instead of a product, lowering friction for cold traffic and segmenting buyers into the right SKU.
how: Build a 4-6 question quiz that routes to your product/bundle (Typeform, Octane AI, Shopify quiz app).
Film a person with the problem + 'which one do I need?' confusion, then screen-record answering the quiz.
End on the results-loading screen and a 'take the free quiz' CTA.
Quiz Walkthrough.closest_existing: Q&A - there the creator answers a question; here the call-to-action is the quiz itself and the ad demos taking it.

BTS vs Final Shot Reveal.definition: Opens on the raw behind-the-scenes setup (rig, tripod, suction mount, studio) capturing a shot, then cuts to the polished final footage it produced, alternating setup vs result a few times and ending on the brand card.
BTS vs Final Shot Reveal.why: Proves the product's output quality directly - the viewer sees exactly what they'd get - ideal for tools that produce a result (camera gear, lighting, editing, beauty tools).
how: Film the product set up doing its job in a plain/messy real environment (the 'how').
Capture or render the clean final result it produces (the 'wow').
Cut setup > result 2-4 times with a 'POV: no crew, just this' caption, end on product + offer.
BTS vs Final Shot Reveal.closest_existing: Product Demo Ads - a demo shows use; this hinges on the contrast reveal between the scrappy setup and the polished output it created.

Torture Test (Try To Break It).definition: The whole ad is a sequence of escalating abuse or stress attempts on the product (flips, jumps, drops, water, weight) with it surviving each one, ending on the verdict shot ('still in / still works') and brand.
Torture Test (Try To Break It).why: Visual proof of durability or fit beats any claim and the escalation keeps people watching to see if it finally fails.
how: List 5-7 increasingly extreme tests relevant to your product's promise (falls out? breaks? leaks?).
Film each in one clean shot with a short caption, hardest test last.
End on the intact product + a 'still going' verdict and offer.
Torture Test (Try To Break It).closest_existing: Product Demo Ads / Challenge - a demo shows normal use; this is a pure escalating stress test where survival is the payoff.

YouTube Reviewer Clip (Borrowed Expert).definition: A horizontal, letterboxed excerpt from an independent long-form YouTube reviewer: often opens on a YouTube-style thumbnail hook, then the reviewer talks through and handles the product with screen recordings/specs, with a branded header bar, closing on 'see full review on YouTube' or a shop end card.
YouTube Reviewer Clip (Borrowed Expert).why: An independent niche expert's real review carries authority no brand claim has; the YouTube look signals unsponsored, in-depth content.
how: Send product to niche YouTubers and license a 30-80s segment of their review.
Keep it horizontal with black bars, add a product-name header and burned-in captions; optional thumbnail-style opener.
Close with end card or 'full review on YouTube + discount code'.
